ZUMA RECRUITS RETURN FROM THE FRONTLINE - A TALE OF TWO MOTHERS

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
We interrogate the return of the Zuma recruits to South Africa - and the consequences for the Zuma and other families

Unique Selling Point:
We have been tracking through WhatsApp conversations two of the 19 Zuma recruits who are returning now from the frontline, after desperate pleas by their families, in particular a woman known as Sis Pumla Zuma, sister-in-law of Jacob Zuma who fought hard to get her family members back from Russia, after seven to eight months of unbearable struggle. The two we have engaged with are Thapelo from Rustenberg who appears to have been caught up in the recruiting while looking for a job; the other is Prince Mzobe, a family member of former President Jacob Zuma.

Summary:
Seventeen recruits return home from seven months on the frontline of Europe's bitter war between Russia and Ukraine, into the arms of their relieved but very stressed families. They return with horrific war stories which are the stuff of nightmares, such is the horror that they have endured as the meat in the meat-grinder of the Russian Army, witnessing the depravity of war and its slaughter. Their families believe they were conned into war by three individuals, the most noteworthy being former President Jacob Zuma's daughter, Duduzile, and his current lover, Siphokazi Xuma. Now that the men are returning, the focus shifts to the recruiters who must face the family members they sent to a possible death. This event has divided the extended Zuma family, with cousin accusing cousin of betrayal. And it has also thrust into the spotlight, the mothers of the men who were sent to Russia, to skill up to become MK security. Another mother, however, who is feeling no joy, is also a family friend of Duduzilem through the child's father. She alleges that Dudu persuaded her to send her boys to Russia for personal training. They had not been heard of since August, presumed dead. And she is very angry.

Further information:
This is a developing story.

Press Release:


Zuma Recruits Return
They were persuaded by people they trusted to join a war on the other side of the world. Now, following presidential negotiations, a group of men have returned after months on the front line, wounded and traumatised by their experience of the bitter war between Russia and Ukraine. As they slip back into the country, the focus is shifting to the politically connected recruiters who hold the secrets to their misadventure. But not all the families are celebrating: one mother, persuaded to send her son to Russia for training, hasn’t heard from him in months. What has become of him? And behind the headlines, what will emerge as a criminal investigation grinds slowly on?
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli


Script:


(Macfarlane Moleli) Allegedly sold, but now, saved. A group of South Africans extracted from the Ukraine- Russia war last month have finally landed on home soil.

(Phumla Zuma) I couldn't believe that I'm really touching my son, after such a long time. This person is coming from a war zone. So I had so many questions.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Arriving at King Shaka airport in Kwazulu-Natal, these men were part of a larger group, allegedly lured to the frontline by members of former president Jacob Zuma’s inner circle.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) I was worried from Day One, you know. They said to me, you you know you're overreacting. You're you need to calm down.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Their going and their coming home has been shrouded in secrecy, confusion and fear. It’s a story that cuts through the heart of one of South Africa’s most powerful political families, and implicates Jacob Zuma’s daughter and family friends.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Sixteen men have returned from the Russia-Ukraine frontlines. They come back with trauma, injuries, and a story that has yet to be fully told.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The misadventure started nine months ago in Nkandla in Kwazulu-Natal, where Jacob Zuma lives among his extended family.

(Macfarlane Moleli) We go there to find his sister-in-law, Phumla Zuma. She’s the mother and grandmother of some of the men who were recruited.

(Phumla Zuma) I had about eight family members in the group of 17. One is my grandchild, and two are my sons, the first and the last one. And those are my only boys.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Phumla says she was approached in June last year by a friend of the former president.

(Phumla Zuma) She said we need men to go to Russia for the Intelligent Unit training and when they come back, they'll get jobs as bodyguard, as security. So as a parent, you think like a a college, they're going to a college.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Ja.

(Phumla Zuma) To be trained

(Macfarlane Moleli) An intelligence training college. Yes

(Macfarlane Moleli) Yes

(Phumla Zuma) So that's what we thought.

(Macfarlane Moleli) In a province blighted by unemployment, this seemed like a lucky break.
We speak to a young man who signed up, excited at an opportunity for funded training in Russia. He asks us to hide his identity.

(“Themba”) I wanted to go to Russia. I wanted to go to the military training. I wanted to go get that money. It was an idea that was brought to us by the people we trusted the most. Everything looked legit, I feel. We didn't have to ask questions.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Trading on family ties and friendships, Umkhonto we Sizwe party member, Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla seems to have been at the forefront of the recruitment drive. It’s alleged that she persuaded two young men from Botswana to join the Nkandla group: Lekgotla Molathlegi and his friend. Zuma-Sambudla was close to Lekgotla’s father – and it was that personal trust that opened the door, says his mother, Kitso.


(Kitso Molatlhegi) I mean, I discussed it with my son. He also was very, very uncomfortable because of the current Ukraine and Russian war, you know. And then he had a call also with Duduzile you know, and was convinced that this is 100% legit and that they will be totally taken care of.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Kitso says Zuma-Sambudla offered Lekgotla a fully funded three-week personal development course: a university place in Russia and a job could follow.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) And Duduzile told me that the visas will be provided, will be done whilst there in Russia. You know, at the time, you're just thinking, okay, she is a Zuma after all, and they're saying that -

(Macfarlane Moleli) She's connected. She's got the network.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) You know, and they're saying that the father has relations with President Putin. So you're like, OK, it should be well taken care of.

(Upsound “Themba”) Everything was moving so quick.
(Macfarlane Moleli) Themba says the men were told to pack light and were sworn to secrecy. They hurried to the airport on July the 8th. Themba never made it – his documents were not in order – but for eight months he tracked his family members across Russia to Ukraine and then right to the frontlines.

(“Themba”) I felt like I was in Russia because they were sending me videos, they were sending me pictures, updating me each and every step that they were going through.

(Macfarlane Moleli) What followed was a parent’s worst nightmare. The 19 men were pressured to sign a contract and just like that, they were soldiers.

(Phumla Zuma) The contract was written in Russian language. They said they are not prepared to sign what they don't understand. Duduzile said, no sign, just sign. It's just an ordinary form. It does - I even signed it as Duduzile. Although they were not happy, they signed, not understanding what they are signing for.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Frantic families were too frightened to speak out. But a little-known politician Thulani Mahlangu offered to help. He was a founding MK party member, but he’d turned against Jacob Zuma’s political party. He made calls to government officials and the Russian Embassy.

(Thulani Mahlangu) I sent them passports of those guys and sent names, sent locations. Some of them, they said, no, they they they they’re in the truck, they are moving. They don’t know where they are going, but they send their location. So we track them that, no, they're all in Ukraine.

(Macfarlane Moleli) By now the new reality was being spelt out in sporadic text messages and voice notes, right from the frontline of the Russia-Ukraine war zone.

(“Themba”) It's land- mines everywhere. It's drones every every now and then, it's bodies left, right and centre. Remember it's winter in Russia, it's it was snowing. So they're not used to those situations.

(Macfarlane Moleli) They are not used to that weather.

(“Themba”) Now they're wearing boots. They're carrying AK47s, you have to run.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The men relayed back that somebody in the recruiting pipeline had been paid - possibly as much as R14 million - for the 19 Africans.

(Phumla Zuma) They started telling us: No, Ma, this is not what we came for here. And we are being told we are their property now. They paid, they bought us, so we have to do whatever they're asking us to do.

(Macfarlane Moleli) So despite being at the forefront of a war that they never signed up for, isn’t it ironic that their most powerful weapon was this - because this is the only thing that kept hope alive for the recruits.

(Macfarlane Moleli) In late January, we were able to make contact with one of the recruits from Nkandla over whatsapp. He begged for our help.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Over the course of a month, we interviewed him online.

(“Themba”) Those guys went through a lot. They suffered. They are traumatized. Even now they it's been, I think, three weeks since they came back, but they don't believe that they're back.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Most of the recruits from Nkandla are recovering physically and psychologically from their eight month ordeal. But the men from Botswana have still not been heard from.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Kitso last heard from her son in late August. Then one of his comrades phoned with unsettling news.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) He told me that the youngest boys from Botswana were taken away from them, and my son wrote them a letter, a note rather, saying: We're being taken away, um, hope to see you on the other side. I don't know what that meant, but he told me that he kept one of his phones, and he said to me that he wants me to have Lekgotla’s phone, and that he hopes he stays alive to come back home and hand over the phone to me. But, if you're looking for answers, call Dudu and Siphokazi and a certain guy called Khoza. They have answers for you. Ask them where your son is.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Photographs of a man called Blessing Khoza appear in this network of whatsapp correspondence, strung between families and their sons. He’s a shadowy figure who appeared to have joined the Russian Army - and we are told he was close to Zuma-Sambudla.

(“Themba”) He was the man in front, and right after the situation uh came out in the news, he disappeared. We never heard from him ever since, ever since then. I think he he was the kingpin I would say.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Is he still missing?

(“Themba”) I doubt he came back to South Africa.

(Macfarlane Moleli) One of the most startling things about all of this is that the alleged recruiters went to family members, possibly knowing that they’re sending them to their deaths.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Phumla appealed to the most powerful person she knew – her brother-in-law Jacob Zuma. Its reported that he went to Russia and wrote a letter but it was not enough. And then one clear message was passed to the families.

(Phumla Zuma) They told us that you’ll have to go to the President of South Africa, because this thing is between the President of Russia and the President. They are the only ones who got the key.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Early last month, Phumla and the families made one last desperate cry for help.

(Phumla Zuma) I’m here today to ask my President to please help us bring our boys back.

(Macfarlane Moleli) And within an hour – but after months of delicate diplomacy – the Presidency made a statement.

(Voice of Vincent Magwenya) President Ramaphosa and President Putin pledge their support to the process of returning South Africans fighting alongside Russian Forces in Ukraine.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Hearing the news, Kitso’s hopes rose.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) Each group that arrives, like I'd constantly be talking to one of them. Have my boys arrived? Have my boys arrived? And they weren't there.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Zuma-Sambudla has long stopped taking Kitso’s calls. She’s publically denied all allegations against her, claiming to be a victim of Blessing Khoza, who appears to have vanished. We try to contact Siphokazi Xuma.

(Voice of Siphokazi Xuma) Hello.

(Macfarlane Moleli) Siphokazi, you are speaking to Macfarlane Moleli from Carte Blanche. We wanted to give you a ROR.

(Macfarlane Moleli) She’s not taking my calls anymore.

(Macfarlane Moleli) In November last year, members of the Zuma family reported the matter to the police, naming Zuma-Sambudla, Jacob Zuma’s friend Siophokazi Xuma, and Blessing Khoza. The authorities have interviewed most of the family members and now the men, as they’ve returned. They have the same evidence we have – and more.

(Macfarlane Moleli) The Hawks have the statements and the multiple messages between the men, their families and the alleged recruiters - so why is this investigation taking so long?

(Macfarlane Moleli) To date, nobody has been charged. One man remains hospitalised in Moscow. The two men from Botswana are still missing, including Kitso’s son.

(Kitso Molatlhegi) I think the one thing I'd say to him is that I'm sorry, you know, for not protecting him as a mother. I really should have trusted my instincts. If by any chance he's not alive, I just still want him back home.

Carte Blanche HD nombuso@carteblanche.co.za 22 March 2026 TX Date: 0000-00-00 Press Release: Zuma Recruits Return They were persuaded by people they trusted to join a war on the other side of the world. Now, following presidential negotiations, a group of men have returned after months on the front line, wounded and traumatised by their experience of the bitter war between Russia and Ukraine. As they slip back into the country, the focus is shifting to the politically connected recruiters who hold the secrets to their misadventure. But not all the families are celebrating: one mother, persuaded to send her son to Russia for training, hasn’t heard from him in months. What has become of him? And behind the headlines, what will emerge as a criminal investigation grinds slowly on? Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli Script: (Macfarlane Moleli) Allegedly sold, but now, saved. A group of South Africans extracted from the Ukraine- Russia war last month have finally landed on home soil. (Phumla Zuma) I couldn't believe that I'm really touching my son, after such a long time. This person is coming from a war zone. So I had so many questions. (Macfarlane Moleli) Arriving at King Shaka airport in Kwazulu-Natal, these men were part of a larger group, allegedly lured to the frontline by members of former president Jacob Zuma’s inner circle. (Kitso Molatlhegi) I was worried from Day One, you know. They said to me, you you know you're overreacting. You're you need to calm down. (Macfarlane Moleli) Their going and their coming home has been shrouded in secrecy, confusion and fear. It’s a story that cuts through the heart of one of South Africa’s most powerful political families, and implicates Jacob Zuma’s daughter and family friends. (Macfarlane Moleli) Sixteen men have returned from the Russia-Ukraine frontlines. They come back with trauma, injuries, and a story that has yet to be fully told. (Macfarlane Moleli) The misadventure started nine months ago in Nkandla in Kwazulu-Natal, where Jacob Zuma lives among his extended family. (Macfarlane Moleli) We go there to find his sister-in-law, Phumla Zuma. She’s the mother and grandmother of some of the men who were recruited. (Phumla Zuma) I had about eight family members in the group of 17. One is my grandchild, and two are my sons, the first and the last one. And those are my only boys. (Macfarlane Moleli) Phumla says she was approached in June last year by a friend of the former president. (Phumla Zuma) She said we need men to go to Russia for the Intelligent Unit training and when they come back, they'll get jobs as bodyguard, as security. So as a parent, you think like a a college, they're going to a college. (Macfarlane Moleli) Ja. (Phumla Zuma) To be trained (Macfarlane Moleli) An intelligence training college. Yes (Macfarlane Moleli) Yes (Phumla Zuma) So that's what we thought. (Macfarlane Moleli) In a province blighted by unemployment, this seemed like a lucky break. We speak to a young man who signed up, excited at an opportunity for funded training in Russia. He asks us to hide his identity. (“Themba”) I wanted to go to Russia. I wanted to go to the military training. I wanted to go get that money. It was an idea that was brought to us by the people we trusted the most. Everything looked legit, I feel. We didn't have to ask questions. (Macfarlane Moleli) Trading on family ties and friendships, Umkhonto we Sizwe party member, Duduzile Zuma-Sambudla seems to have been at the forefront of the recruitment drive. It’s alleged that she persuaded two young men from Botswana to join the Nkandla group: Lekgotla Molathlegi and his friend. Zuma-Sambudla was close to Lekgotla’s father – and it was that personal trust that opened the door, says his mother, Kitso. (Kitso Molatlhegi) I mean, I discussed it with my son. He also was very, very uncomfortable because of the current Ukraine and Russian war, you know. And then he had a call also with Duduzile you know, and was convinced that this is 100% legit and that they will be totally taken care of. (Macfarlane Moleli) Kitso says Zuma-Sambudla offered Lekgotla a fully funded three-week personal development course: a university place in Russia and a job could follow. (Kitso Molatlhegi) And Duduzile told me that the visas will be provided, will be done whilst there in Russia. You know, at the time, you're just thinking, okay, she is a Zuma after all, and they're saying that - (Macfarlane Moleli) She's connected. She's got the network. (Kitso Molatlhegi) You know, and they're saying that the father has relations with President Putin. So you're like, OK, it should be well taken care of. (Upsound “Themba”) Everything was moving so quick. (Macfarlane Moleli) Themba says the men were told to pack light and were sworn to secrecy. They hurried to the airport on July the 8th. Themba never made it – his documents were not in order – but for eight months he tracked his family members across Russia to Ukraine and then right to the frontlines. (“Themba”) I felt like I was in Russia because they were sending me videos, they were sending me pictures, updating me each and every step that they were going through. (Macfarlane Moleli) What followed was a parent’s worst nightmare. The 19 men were pressured to sign a contract and just like that, they were soldiers. (Phumla Zuma) The contract was written in Russian language. They said they are not prepared to sign what they don't understand. Duduzile said, no sign, just sign. It's just an ordinary form. It does - I even signed it as Duduzile. Although they were not happy, they signed, not understanding what they are signing for. (Macfarlane Moleli) Frantic families were too frightened to speak out. But a little-known politician Thulani Mahlangu offered to help. He was a founding MK party member, but he’d turned against Jacob Zuma’s political party. He made calls to government officials and the Russian Embassy. (Thulani Mahlangu) I sent them passports of those guys and sent names, sent locations. Some of them, they said, no, they they they they’re in the truck, they are moving. They don’t know where they are going, but they send their location. So we track them that, no, they're all in Ukraine. (Macfarlane Moleli) By now the new reality was being spelt out in sporadic text messages and voice notes, right from the frontline of the Russia-Ukraine war zone. (“Themba”) It's land- mines everywhere. It's drones every every now and then, it's bodies left, right and centre. Remember it's winter in Russia, it's it was snowing. So they're not used to those situations. (Macfarlane Moleli) They are not used to that weather. (“Themba”) Now they're wearing boots. They're carrying AK47s, you have to run. (Macfarlane Moleli) The men relayed back that somebody in the recruiting pipeline had been paid - possibly as much as R14 million - for the 19 Africans. (Phumla Zuma) They started telling us: No, Ma, this is not what we came for here. And we are being told we are their property now. They paid, they bought us, so we have to do whatever they're asking us to do. (Macfarlane Moleli) So despite being at the forefront of a war that they never signed up for, isn’t it ironic that their most powerful weapon was this - because this is the only thing that kept hope alive for the recruits. (Macfarlane Moleli) In late January, we were able to make contact with one of the recruits from Nkandla over whatsapp. He begged for our help. (Macfarlane Moleli) Over the course of a month, we interviewed him online. (“Themba”) Those guys went through a lot. They suffered. They are traumatized. Even now they it's been, I think, three weeks since they came back, but they don't believe that they're back. (Macfarlane Moleli) Most of the recruits from Nkandla are recovering physically and psychologically from their eight month ordeal. But the men from Botswana have still not been heard from. (Macfarlane Moleli) Kitso last heard from her son in late August. Then one of his comrades phoned with unsettling news. (Kitso Molatlhegi) He told me that the youngest boys from Botswana were taken away from them, and my son wrote them a letter, a note rather, saying: We're being taken away, um, hope to see you on the other side. I don't know what that meant, but he told me that he kept one of his phones, and he said to me that he wants me to have Lekgotla’s phone, and that he hopes he stays alive to come back home and hand over the phone to me. But, if you're looking for answers, call Dudu and Siphokazi and a certain guy called Khoza. They have answers for you. Ask them where your son is. (Macfarlane Moleli) Photographs of a man called Blessing Khoza appear in this network of whatsapp correspondence, strung between families and their sons. He’s a shadowy figure who appeared to have joined the Russian Army - and we are told he was close to Zuma-Sambudla. (“Themba”) He was the man in front, and right after the situation uh came out in the news, he disappeared. We never heard from him ever since, ever since then. I think he he was the kingpin I would say. (Macfarlane Moleli) Is he still missing? (“Themba”) I doubt he came back to South Africa. (Macfarlane Moleli) One of the most startling things about all of this is that the alleged recruiters went to family members, possibly knowing that they’re sending them to their deaths. (Macfarlane Moleli) Phumla appealed to the most powerful person she knew – her brother-in-law Jacob Zuma. Its reported that he went to Russia and wrote a letter but it was not enough. And then one clear message was passed to the families. (Phumla Zuma) They told us that you’ll have to go to the President of South Africa, because this thing is between the President of Russia and the President. They are the only ones who got the key. (Macfarlane Moleli) Early last month, Phumla and the families made one last desperate cry for help. (Phumla Zuma) I’m here today to ask my President to please help us bring our boys back. (Macfarlane Moleli) And within an hour – but after months of delicate diplomacy – the Presidency made a statement. (Voice of Vincent Magwenya) President Ramaphosa and President Putin pledge their support to the process of returning South Africans fighting alongside Russian Forces in Ukraine. (Macfarlane Moleli) Hearing the news, Kitso’s hopes rose. (Kitso Molatlhegi) Each group that arrives, like I'd constantly be talking to one of them. Have my boys arrived? Have my boys arrived? And they weren't there. (Macfarlane Moleli) Zuma-Sambudla has long stopped taking Kitso’s calls. She’s publically denied all allegations against her, claiming to be a victim of Blessing Khoza, who appears to have vanished. We try to contact Siphokazi Xuma. (Voice of Siphokazi Xuma) Hello. (Macfarlane Moleli) Siphokazi, you are speaking to Macfarlane Moleli from Carte Blanche. We wanted to give you a ROR. (Macfarlane Moleli) She’s not taking my calls anymore. (Macfarlane Moleli) In November last year, members of the Zuma family reported the matter to the police, naming Zuma-Sambudla, Jacob Zuma’s friend Siophokazi Xuma, and Blessing Khoza. The authorities have interviewed most of the family members and now the men, as they’ve returned. They have the same evidence we have – and more. (Macfarlane Moleli) The Hawks have the statements and the multiple messages between the men, their families and the alleged recruiters - so why is this investigation taking so long? (Macfarlane Moleli) To date, nobody has been charged. One man remains hospitalised in Moscow. The two men from Botswana are still missing, including Kitso’s son. (Kitso Molatlhegi) I think the one thing I'd say to him is that I'm sorry, you know, for not protecting him as a mother. I really should have trusted my instincts. If by any chance he's not alive, I just still want him back home.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): We interrogate the return of the Zuma recruits to South Africa - and the consequences for the Zuma and other families
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We have been tracking through WhatsApp conversations two of the 19 Zuma recruits who are returning now from the frontline, after desperate pleas by their families, in particular a woman known as Sis Pumla Zuma, sister-in-law of Jacob Zuma who fought hard to get her family members back from Russia, after seven to eight months of unbearable struggle. The two we have engaged with are Thapelo from Rustenberg who appears to have been caught up in the recruiting while looking for a job; the other is Prince Mzobe, a family member of former President Jacob Zuma.
metadata.Summary: Seventeen recruits return home from seven months on the frontline of Europe's bitter war between Russia and Ukraine, into the arms of their relieved but very stressed families. They return with horrific war stories which are the stuff of nightmares, such is the horror that they have endured as the meat in the meat-grinder of the Russian Army, witnessing the depravity of war and its slaughter. Their families believe they were conned into war by three individuals, the most noteworthy being former President Jacob Zuma's daughter, Duduzile, and his current lover, Siphokazi Xuma. Now that the men are returning, the focus shifts to the recruiters who must face the family members they sent to a possible death. This event has divided the extended Zuma family, with cousin accusing cousin of betrayal. And it has also thrust into the spotlight, the mothers of the men who were sent to Russia, to skill up to become MK security. Another mother, however, who is feeling no joy, is also a family friend of Duduzilem through the child's father. She alleges that Dudu persuaded her to send her boys to Russia for personal training. They had not been heard of since August, presumed dead. And she is very angry.
